body: A few families settle at Cnoc dhìreach to tend Tuam Cnoc dhìreach after the Keeper's burial. The Hall pays them in coal, a handful each a season, the only payment in coal the Law ever allows.

title: Eilidh nic Ìomhair keeps the flame
body: The nine hearths choose a Keeper from outside the house of Muireach for the first time: Eilidh nic Ìomhair, of Dùn dhearg. Sliochd Mhuirich refuses for a season, then yields at Dùn ìseal, on the condition that the stone cup never leaves Talla na Lasrach.

title: The Four Houses sworn
body: Under Eilidh nic Ìomhair the office of Keeper is bound to four houses of custody: Sliochd Mhuirich of Dùn ìseal, Sliochd Ìomhair of Dùn dhearg, Sliochd Thormoid of Seann Dunn and Sliochd Raghnaill of Seann Tarr. The other hearths keep their seats on the council, but lose their claim to the flame. Most of the later nobility of the island descends from one of the four, or says it does.

title: The house of Tormod at Seann Dunn
body: Sliochd Thormoid raises a hall and a shrine at Seann Dunn, facing the mountain across the river. A lamp of coal burns in the shrine at the Law's measure. The other houses complain that the measure of Seann Dunn is always the fullest.

title: The house of Raghnall at Seann Tarr
body: Sliochd Raghnaill takes for its seat Seann Tarr on the north-eastern coast, the town whose household was first sentenced under the Law. The house keeps boats and not galleries, and grows rich on the fishing.

title: Round Eilean dhubh
body: Boats of Sliochd Raghnaill sail round Eilean dhubh and come home, the first voyage made to see a coast and not to fish it. The house's songs name the steersman Tormod Ruadh. He brings back word of rock and birds, and of having gone, and of nothing else.

title: The outlaws of the north-west waters
body: Households stripped of their right under the Law for a third offence take to boats, live off the north-western waters, and raid the fishing strands. They are called spùinneadairean, plunderers, and the name stays with those waters after them.

title: The boat lost off the north-west
body: A fishing boat out of Baile chrom is lost in calm water off the north-western coast. The two men who swim home say that something rose under it. Each year thereafter the boat's village keeps a wake for it. Of the thing they saw no more is told.

title: The fire at Baile chrom relit
body: After the loss the fishers of Baile chrom light the old beacon on the point again, fed with driftwood as the Law requires. From it comes Taigh-solais Baile chrom.

title: Seann Bhrenn resettled
body: Fishers from the north side of the mountain settle the harbour of Seann Bhrenn on the northern coast and keep its old name, as the western settlers kept Seann Warr's. They find a stone quay under the silt and use it.

title: The ancestor-cairn at Cathair naomh
body: The people of Cathair naomh in the north raise a cairn for their dead on the hill above the town, and bring it a stone at every burial. It is the greatest ancestor-cairn in the north, and it grows still.

title: The panthers let pass
body: The crossing of the great cats is found to run straight over the carriers' southern road. Eilidh nic Ìomhair rules that no panther may be killed on the road in its season, and the carriers wait in the waypoint houses until the crossing is done. The rule is kept, for it costs the carriers only time.

title: The granaries of Dùn dhearg
body: Sliochd Ìomhair builds stone granaries at Dùn dhearg and fills them from the lowland fields, holding grain against the storm season as the old custom of sharing asks. So the house gains what the Hall never had: people who owe it their bread.

title: Baile Mòr dhomhain at the foot of the pass
body: Carriers who take the Hall's baskets north over the high pass settle at its southern foot, where Baile Mòr dhomhain now stands, to rest their beasts before the climb. The town lives by the pass, and by little else.

title: The reverent centuries
body: Generation after generation mines the same small measure and burns the same small measure, and the people neither grow nor dwindle. The rolls call them the reverent centuries.

title: Coinneach Mòr mac Tormoid keeps the flame
body: Coinneach Mòr mac Tormoid of Seann Dunn becomes the first Keeper of Sliochd Thormoid. He keeps the flame longer than any Keeper before him, and changes nothing while he keeps it.

title: The shepherds of Achadh chaol
body: Shepherds settle the upland fields at Achadh chaol in the north-east and send their wool down to the harbours. Their headman sits one season on the council at Dùn ìseal, is found to hold no hearth-right, and goes home.

title: The Keepers' count of the old places
body: Coinneach Mòr sends walkers to list the ruins of the old people. They bring back Làrach an Dùin-fhaire, Làrach an Dùin, Làrach an Teampaill and the standing stones. The list says who does not own each place, and not who built it; the Keepers rule that it shall not guess.

title: The fence round Carragh Cnoc bheag
body: The people of Cnoc bheag set a ring of stakes round the old standing stone above their town, that the cattle may not rub against it. Every generation after renews the ring. The stone is never moved.

title: The bath-house at Muileann ruadh
body: A roofed bath-house is built over the warm springs below Muileann ruadh, with sleeping-places for the sick and their bearers. The Hall appoints a keeper of the springs, who tends them in the name of Dian Cècht, the healer. It is the first office the Hall makes that has nothing to do with the coal.

title: The silver weights of Muileann chiar
body: The silversmiths of Muileann chiar cast a set of weights, the least the weight of a barley-corn and the greatest that of a newborn lamb. Every trader on the carriers' roads comes to use them, and for the rest of the age a thing weighed at Muileann chiar is said to be weighed fairly.

title: The market under the Hall
body: A market is held under the walls of the Hall at Dùn ìseal on the four quarter days, Samhain, Là Fhèill Brìde, Bealltainn and Lùnastal, when the households of the eastern hills come up with their dues. Hides, venison, charcoal, honey and the silver of Muileann chiar change hands there on the new weights. The Keepers allow no coal to be sold on their ground, and none is.

title: The stag's people at Cnoc bhàn
body: A house of the stag's people is founded at Cnoc bhàn, north of the mountain, and after the long exclusion takes cutters again. Its teachers keep the question of Sìleas nic Coinnich as she left it: why does the coal show its colours for one hand and not another?

title: Seonaid Chiar reopens the galleries to the stag's people
body: Seonaid Chiar, Keeper of the house of Muireach, lets cutters trained by the stag's people back into the galleries at Dùn ìseal, sworn to ask nothing of the vein aloud. The Hall's roll calls it a reconciling. The school remembers it as a truce.

title: Cathair mhòr walled
body: The people of Cathair mhòr on the southern coast build a wall of fitted stone about their headland town, the first town wall on the island. What they feared no one has told.

title: Ceann leathan's fish-market
body: Ceann leathan becomes the market of the southern fishing and sends dried fish inland along the carriers' paths. Its harbour-master keeps tallies on notched sticks. Several are kept at Muileann chaol, the oldest counted things in its keeping.

title: The shrine at Inis thais
body: A shrine to the ancestors lost at sea is raised at Inis thais on the western coast. Its keepers burn their season's handful on the shore and not indoors, so that the drowned, gone west over the sea, may see it.

title: Cuan shean's salt-pans
body: The people of Cuan shean on the western coast dig salt-pans on the flats below the town and boil sea-water over peat. Their salt goes inland along the western road and keeps the fish of half the island.

title: Salt-carriers on the heath above Baile fhiadhaich
body: Salt-carriers from Cuan shean settle on the western heath above Baile fhiadhaich, by a stream that runs all summer. The heath about it is not worth the plough, and its people keep goats.

title: The sunny house
body: A waypoint house is built on the eastern road where the carriers from Cnoc leathan meet the southern coast path, on the site of An Taigh-òsta Grianach. It faces south, and from the first is known for its warmth, which is all its name has ever meant.

title: Cnoc leathan's market
body: Cnoc leathan, at the eastern end of the road past the sunny house, becomes the market town of the south-eastern hills. Its carriers' guild holds the right to carry for the Hall on the stretch down to the coast.

title: The fall in the high gallery
body: A roof falls in the highest gallery at Dùn ìseal and kills four cutters. The gallery is walled up and left. Seonaid Chiar orders props of oak set in every gallery after, and for the first time the Hall spends timber on the mountain.

title: Cathair dhomhain founded
body: Carriers settled at the mouth of the western road raise a town on the rise above the harbour and name it Cathair dhomhain. Its shrine keeps the Law's measure strictly, and its people are proud of it.

title: A fishing town at Cathair dhearg
body: The old settlement of the Red Hill, shrunk to a small fishing town, grows again at the western bridge-foot on the Abhainn dhomhain, a little above its meeting with the Abhainn gheal below Loch chrom. The ground is afterwards called Cathair dhearg, for its red stone. As yet it is a place carriers pass through on the way to somewhere else.

title: Goraidh mac Ìomhair called rìgh
body: At Dùn dhearg the lowland households who eat from the granaries of Sliochd Ìomhair begin to call its head, Goraidh mac Ìomhair, their rìgh, their king. No ruler of the lowlands was so called before him. Goraidh claims nothing over the vein, and is careful to tell the Hall so.

title: The division of keeping
body: The council at Dùn ìseal and Goraidh mac Ìomhair agree on a division. The Keeper keeps the flame and the galleries; the rìgh keeps the roads, the granaries and the peace of the lowlands. The rìgh may not enter the galleries, and the Keeper may not raise spears. On this division the island is governed for the rest of the age.

title: Goraidh Mòr's hall
body: Goraidh mac Ìomhair, called Goraidh Mòr, builds a timber hall on the hill at Dùn dhearg, with a granary at each corner. Its post-holes could still be seen when the surveyors of the Library walked the hill, and they measured and drew them.

title: The first road-toll
body: Goraidh Mòr sets a toll on the carriers' roads, one fish in twenty or its worth, to pay the road-guards and keep up the bridges. The keepers of the waypoint houses gather it, and keep a share of it, and the rolls say so.

title: Mòrag of the Roads
body: Mòrag nic Ghoraidh takes the hall at Dùn dhearg after her father Goraidh Mòr. She is called Mòrag nan Rathad, Mòrag of the Roads, for in her first years she walks every carriers' road on the island and orders the bad stretches made anew.

title: The golden house
body: Mòrag nan Rathad has a waypoint house built on the road north of Seann Dunn, on the site of An Taigh-seinnse Òir, to shorten the carriers' stage from the coast to the mountain. It is the first waypoint house raised by a ruler and not by a family.

title: The bridge-foot rebuilt
body: At the bidding of Mòrag nan Rathad the western crossing of the Abhainn dhomhain is rebuilt in wider stone, so that two laden carriers can pass on it. The hearth-sign of Ailean Clachair is cut again in its keystone. From this time the town at the bridge-foot begins to grow.

title: Dòmhnall Crùbach
body: Dòmhnall Crùbach, Dòmhnall the Lame, follows his mother Mòrag at Dùn dhearg. He cannot walk the roads as she did, and rules through the keepers of the waypoint houses, who grow mighty in his reign.

title: The waypoint-keepers of Ceann mhin
body: In the reign of Dòmhnall Crùbach the keepers of the waypoint houses about the harbour town of Ceann mhin take the gathering of the road-toll into their own hands and pay the rìgh what they judge fair. Their judgement is generous to themselves, and the rolls keep the sums.

title: Baile àrsaidh on the western heath
body: Settlers from Cathair dhomhain take the wet heath of the west coast and found Baile àrsaidh, where the soil is thin and the yellow scorpions thick. They swear their oaths on a scorpion's sting kept in a box, and their neighbours think it a strange custom.

title: The storm at Seann Chwen
body: A storm drives the sea over the harbour at Seann Chwen and takes the boats and a third of the houses. The Keeper sends the Hall's grain from Dùn ìseal, and Dòmhnall Crùbach sends his from Dùn dhearg. The survivors remember that the Hall's came first.

title: The stag-letters
body: At Muileann chiar in the far east the teachers of the stag's people make the cutters' tally-notches into signs for sounds, so that a teaching may be kept without a teacher. These are the first letters the Dia-thìrich use: the ogham, which the druids call the gift of Ogma. From them come nearly all the later hands of the island.

title: The letters set against the obelisk
body: Scholars of the stag carry their new letters to Carragh Cnoc bheag and set them beside the marks on the obelisk. They match nothing. The scholars write that the stone's makers were not their teachers, and that is the first thing the Dia-thìrich ever write of the old people.

title: Sìleas Dhonn
body: Sìleas Dhonn, niece of Dòmhnall Crùbach, holds Dùn dhearg after him. In her reign the keepers of the waypoint houses are bidden to render account of the tolls at her hall once a year, and several of them do.

title: The lords of Caol leathan
body: The harbour town of Caol leathan in the south-west grows rich on the western fishing and the southern end of the carriers' road. Its leading family, under Lachlann Ciar, takes the road-toll for itself and sends none of it to Dùn dhearg.

title: Iain Garbh
body: Iain Garbh, Iain the Rough, son of Sìleas Dhonn, takes the hall at Dùn dhearg and demands the western tolls of Caol leathan. Lachlann Ciar sends back a basket of fish-bones.

title: The War of the Roads begins at Muileann òg
body: Iain Garbh marches west with the road-guards and the lowland levies, and burns the toll-house at Muileann òg that the men of Lachlann Ciar had taken. It is the first war of Dia-thìreach against Dia-thìreach. The Hall will bless neither side.

title: Uisdean mac Ruairidh's refusal
body: The Keeper Uisdean mac Ruairidh refuses the messengers of Iain Garbh at Dùn ìseal the Hall's handful for the warband's hearths, saying that the flame does not warm men who go out to kill. The warband winters on peat. Iain Garbh never forgives the Hall, and never enters it.

title: The fight at Àth fhiadhaich
body: The men of Caol leathan meet the levies of Iain Garbh at the ford of Àth fhiadhaich and hold it for a day before they give way. Forty lie dead of both sides. Long afterwards the carriers call it the ford of the forty.

title: Baile ghlas burned
body: The men of Lachlann Ciar, falling back on Caol leathan, burn Baile ghlas, that the levies of Iain Garbh may find no grain. Its people walk to Cathair dhomhain, and many never return.

title: Baile chiar holds
body: Baile chiar, south of the western bridge-foot, shuts its gate on both hosts in the War of the Roads and feeds the burned-out folk of Baile ghlas through the winter. Neither side forgives it, and neither attacks it.

title: The siege of Caol leathan
body: Iain Garbh shuts Caol leathan in from the land for a season, but its boats bring in fish from the sea, and the harbour he cannot close. His levies begin to go home for the harvest, and the siege ends without an assault.

title: The peace at Mòr nic Dhùghaill's house
body: Iain Garbh and Lachlann Ciar meet under the roof of the waypoint house that is afterwards Am Buabhall Fortanach, where by the road-peace neither may draw. Caol leathan keeps half its tolls and sends half to Dùn dhearg, and Lachlann Ciar swears to the Law before the Keeper's witness. So the War of the Roads ends in a house built to feed carriers.

title: The wolf-sworn of Caol leathan
body: Men who fought for Caol leathan become its road-guards and swear their watch on a white stone carved as a wolf, kept at the town gate. They call themselves the wolf-sworn. Later ages read more into the stone than they did, and call it Lia Fàil.

title: Caol fhiadhaich rebuilt
body: Caol fhiadhaich on the south-western shore had sent its boats to feed Caol leathan through the siege. In thanks Lachlann Ciar gives it a share of the western tolls, and with it the town builds a harbour wall.

title: Death of Iain Garbh
body: Iain Garbh dies at Dùn dhearg. His daughter Catrìona buries him in the floor of the hall and not on the slope at Dùn ìseal, and the Hall does not ask for him.

title: Catrìona Ghlic
body: Catrìona Ghlic, Catrìona the Wise, rules from Dùn dhearg. She sends her own son to sit a season with the flame, the first child of the royal house to do so since the division of keeping. By the end of her reign the Hall and the hall are on speaking terms again.

title: The house on the northern road
body: Catrìona Ghlic has a waypoint house built on the northern road above Inis mhòr, on the site of An Leòmhann Buidhe. It serves the carriers who take the Hall's baskets to the northern households and bring back wool.

title: The house on the cold road
body: A stone house is built on the open moor, on the road between Baile Mòr dhomhain and the northern coast, on the site of An Taigh-seinnse Reòta, for carriers caught by snow. The Hall pays its keepers in grain and the crown in cloth, and they complain of both.

title: Inis mhòr grows
body: The river port of Inis mhòr in the north becomes the gathering-place of the northern wool trade and outgrows every other northern town. Its people ask Catrìona Ghlic for a road-guard of their own, and are given one.

title: The market at the fords of Baile Mòr dhomhain
body: The lords of the deep river set a market at Baile Mòr dhomhain, where the carriers' road from the south meets the paths down from the hill pastures. Cattle, sheep, horses, hides and the white stone of the hills are sold at the fords on the day after each new moon, and the lords take one fleece in forty from the sellers.

title: Muileann shean on the northern road
body: A mill is built at Muileann shean on the northern road, to grind the grain the carriers bring over the pass, and a town grows round it. The Hall pays the miller in grain, and he pays the rìgh's toll in flour.

title: The unremembered rulers
body: Eleven rulers hold Dùn dhearg between Catrìona Ghlic and Ealasaid Chiar. The later king-list gives their names and their order, and nothing more. For the same years the Keepers' roll gives five Keepers, and of them too only the names.

title: Tormod Scrìobhaiche learns the letters
body: Tormod mac Iain, a younger son of the house of Tormod, is sent east to Muileann chiar to learn the stag-letters. He is the first of the royal kin to read, and for the rest of his life he is called Tormod Scrìobhaiche, Tormod the Writer.

title: Ealasaid Chiar
body: Ealasaid Chiar takes the hall at Dùn dhearg and brings Tormod Scrìobhaiche there as her clerk. She bids him set down in order the name of every ruler of the hall that the reciters can give him.

title: The first written king-list
body: Rulers are first set down by name, and no longer only remembered in tales. The rolls of succession in every later age are kept after this pattern.

title: The contents of Tormod's roll
body: Tormod Scrìobhaiche's roll, kept in the hall at Dùn dhearg, runs from Goraidh Mòr to Ealasaid Chiar. The earlier names he has from the reciters and the later from living memory, and he marks which are which. In three places it differs from the Keepers' spoken roll; Tormod writes down both readings and does not choose.

title: The Keepers' roll written down
body: Shamed, in the Hall's own words, by the rìgh's clerk, the Keepers have their spoken roll written in stag-letters at Dùn ìseal. It begins with Beathag Bhàn, and it is longer than Tormod's by several centuries.

title: The watchers of the dark wood
body: A small company settles at the edge of Coille Naomh Cnoc bheag, the wood never cleared, and keeps watch for a black horned beast that they say walks in it. The people of Cathair dhearg call them the wood-watchers. None of their own accounts is older than Òrd Mhacha, the order of Macha, which afterwards claims them and takes the beast for a sign of Dubh Sainglenn, the black horse.

title: The wood-watchers in the stag's grove
body: Wood-watchers come east and cut a black-barked tree in Coille Naomh Muileann chiar, saying that the beast had shown it to them. The stag's people call it theft from a place of teaching. Both sides send to Dùn dhearg and to Dùn ìseal.

title: The stag's people claim the dark wood
body: In answer the stag's people send teachers west to hold their lessons in Coille Naomh Cnoc bheag, saying that the first stag came from there. Now each side claims both woods, and in either wood the two companies meet and do not speak.

title: The holy-wood dispute
body: Rival rites contend for Coille Naomh Muileann chiar and Coille Naomh Cnoc bheag, the first such strife that is remembered. It is settled by dividing the keeping of the woods, and no side is judged the victor.

title: The boundary stones of the woods
body: The woods are divided at Dùn dhearg before Fearchar Òg, rìgh after Ealasaid Chiar, and the Keeper Calum Liath. The stag's people keep the eastern wood and the wood-watchers the western, and each may walk in the other's wood unarmed and without cutting. Boundary stones are set at the edges of both woods with the terms cut on them in stag-letters. Two of the eastern stones remain.

title: Calum Liath's surveyors
body: The Keeper Calum Liath sends cutters with knotted cords and lamps into every gallery at Dùn ìseal, to follow the vein as far as it can be followed and mark where it thickens and thins. The work keeps the cutters from the coal for three seasons, and the households go short to pay for it.

title: The measuring of the vein
body: For the first time men try to reckon how much coal the mountain holds. Their reckoning proves far too hopeful.

title: The reckoning of the cords
body: The reckoning of Calum Liath is cut on a slab in the Hall at Dùn ìseal: the mountain can give every household its handful for more generations than there are grains in the granaries of Dùn dhearg. It is read out at the council and heard in silence, and the Hall takes the silence for assent.

title: The deaths in the lower gallery
body: Two youths of the nine hearths, sent into the lower gallery at Dùn ìseal without a Keeper's cutter to guide them, break the wrong face and are crushed. They had been less than a season in the galleries. Their families ask the council what the Hall owes them, and the council has no answer.

title: The apprentice-binding custom
body: Young Dia-thìrich are first bound for seven years to a master of the vein's custody before they may go near the coal themselves. Every later guild of the mines is shaped on this binding.

title: Oighrig Bhàn's first bound
body: Oighrig Bhàn, Keeper after Calum Liath, binds the first twelve apprentices under the new custom at Dùn ìseal, each to a master cutter by name. They swear on the stone cup to serve seven years before they touch the vein. Four of the twelve are afterwards Keepers, which is the best that can be said for the custom.

title: The stag's people take apprentices
body: The house of the stag's people at Cnoc bhàn takes the seven years for its own cutters and adds a rule: an apprentice keeps a written account of every stroke, and the account is read. These strike-books are the school's chief record for the rest of the age.

title: The long reign of Fearchar Òg
body: Fearchar Òg, who divided the woods, rules long at Dùn dhearg and is remembered chiefly for dying old. He was named Òg, the young, for coming to the hall as a boy, and the name stuck.

title: The silver tokens
body: The clerks of Fearchar Òg begin to pay the road-guards in small silver rings of the Muileann chiar weight, stamped with the hall's mark. It is the first payment in metal by any ruler on Dia-thìr. The rings travel further than the guards do.

title: The toll-house at Àth ghlas
body: A toll-house is built on the ford at Àth ghlas, where the southern road crosses the river toward Ceann leathan, and the road-guards are paid there in the new silver rings. Its keeper is the first sent from the rìgh's hall, and not chosen in the place.

title: The road-guards' games at Ceann leathan
body: The road-guards of the south begin to meet each year at Ceann leathan and fight with blunted staves for a silver ring. The meeting outlives its purpose, and on its field Còmhrag Ceann leathan is afterwards fought. The first winner whose name is kept is a woman, Mòrag Dhubh of Cnoc mhòr.

title: The fair at Muileann òg
body: Muileann òg, burned in the War of the Roads, is rebuilt as a market town. A fair is held there each harvest at Lùnastal for the trade of the western and southern roads, and from it Fèill Muileann òg descends.

title: The landing on the Abhainn uaine
body: A landing for river-boats is built on the Abhainn uaine at the place since called Cidhe Beag, so that the grain of the lowlands may go upriver by boat and not on carriers' backs. The carriers of the eastern road protest to Fearchar Òg, and lose.

title: The river-boats
body: Flat river-boats of hide over withy begin to carry grain and salt fish up the Abhainn uaine from the landing at Cidhe Beag. The boatmen form a fellowship of their own, sworn on a paddle, and vie with the carriers for the Hall's baskets.

title: The boatmen of Muileann chrom
body: Muileann chrom, up the valley from the landing at Cidhe Beag, becomes the home of the river-boatmen and their fellowship. Its yards build the flat hide boats for every river of the island.

title: Beathag Mhòr
body: Beathag Mhòr, great-granddaughter of Fearchar Òg, takes the hall at Dùn dhearg. The list calls her banrìgh, queen, the first so called, and not rìgh with a woman's name after it; the change of word is the list's own.

title: The fleece-measure of Baile Mòr fhionn
body: The lords of the western plain hold a market at Baile Mòr fhionn and make the fleece of a grown ewe its measure. Grain, wine, cattle and the horses of the plain are all priced in fleeces. The silver rings of Muileann chiar are taken there too, but reckoned in wool.

title: The hall moves to Cathair dhearg
body: Beathag Mhòr moves her hall from Dùn dhearg to the town at the western bridge-foot, Cathair dhearg, to sit where the roads, the river and the western harbours meet. Dùn dhearg keeps the old granaries and the graves of the house of Ìomhar. From this reign Cathair dhearg is the seat of rule on Dia-thìr, whatever else changes.

title: Dùn dhearg after the move
body: Dùn dhearg, left behind, keeps its granaries and its pride. Its people go on calling it the rìgh's hill, and for many generations its reeves will send their accounts to Cathair dhearg in no hand but their own.

title: The red hall
body: Beathag Mhòr's hall at Cathair dhearg is built on the rise above the harbour, of the red stone that names the town. Its foundations lie under the later citadel. The masons cut the hearth-sign in its lintel as though it were a bridge.

title: Cathair dhomhain against Cathair dhearg
body: The harbour of Cathair dhomhain, older and larger, grudges the new seat on its doorstep and refuses the queen's toll on its boats. Beathag Mhòr grants it a charter of its own tolls. The two towns, a few miles apart, are rivals for the rest of the age.

title: Disputed hands
body: The council at Dùn ìseal is asked to judge more quarrels over the right to the handful than over anything else: new households, divided households, households that claim descent from one of the nine hearths without proof. Dùghall mac Raghnaill, Keeper after Oighrig Bhàn, asks the queen for a counting.

title: Beathag Mhòr orders the count
body: Beathag Mhòr and Dùghall mac Raghnaill agree that every household on the island claiming the handful shall be counted, its right proved or refused, and its name written. The clerks at Cathair dhearg are to write, and the Keepers to judge.

title: The waypoint houses as counting-houses
body: The counters make their stations at the waypoint houses, for every household on the island lies within a day of one. The keepers of the houses feed the counters at the queen's cost, and in the houses the count is afterwards remembered as a good year.

title: The census of hands
body: The households that hold the old right to burn the coal are counted across the whole island for the first time. So it is shown that the burning of the coal was already rationed by rule.

title: The count of hands
body: The rolls of the count, kept at Cathair dhearg, give eleven thousand four hundred households holding the right, and some two thousand whose claims were refused. The refused are written on a roll of their own, and it is that roll later generations search when they would prove an ancestor's standing.

title: The refused of Seann Tarr
body: Most of the refused households of the north-eastern coast are fisher-families about Seann Tarr who had never burned coal at all, and now find they have no right to begin. Sliochd Raghnaill takes up their cause at the council and loses. The fisher-families burn peat and say it is warmer.

title: The light at Baile ìseal
body: The old beacon on the eastern point at Baile ìseal is rebuilt, kept with driftwood and seal fat as the Law requires, to bring the fishing boats of the eastern coast home in the dark. From it comes Taigh-solais Baile ìseal.

title: The light at Muileann bheag
body: The old beacon on the northern headland at Muileann bheag is rebuilt; from it comes Taigh-solais Muileann bheag. Its keepers are fisher-families of the north-west, who pay no toll to Cathair dhearg in return for keeping it.

title: The light at Àth dhearg
body: Sliochd Raghnaill rebuilds the old beacon on the north-eastern cape at Àth dhearg, to mark the way in toward Seann Tarr. From it comes Taigh-solais Àth dhearg.

title: Death of Beathag Mhòr
body: Beathag Mhòr dies at Cathair dhearg and by her own command is carried back to Dùn dhearg to lie among the house of Ìomhar. No royal journey before it was so long.

title: Ruairidh Liath
body: Ruairidh Liath, son of Beathag Mhòr, rules from Cathair dhearg. He is grey already when he takes the hall, and his byname is the list's one jest.

title: The Silver Feud begins
body: Ruairidh Liath demands one ring in five of the silver taken at Muileann chiar, saying the tokens that pay his guards should cost him nothing. Sliochd Fhearchair, the silversmiths' house, answers with Muireach Liath's ruling: silver is not holy, and so not the crown's either. They close the workings sooner than pay.

title: The closing of the silver
body: For three seasons no silver leaves Muileann chiar. The road-guards go unpaid, the fair at Muileann òg trades in grain again, and the tolls of the eastern road go ungathered. It is called the Silver Feud, though no one is killed in it.

title: The Keeper's judgment on the silver
body: At the asking of both sides the Keeper Dùghall mac Raghnaill rules at Dùn ìseal that the words of Muireach Liath stand, and silver is not the mountain's; but also that the crown keeps the roads the silver travels. Ruairidh Liath takes one ring in ten, Sliochd Fhearchair opens the workings again, and each calls it a victory.

title: The Muileann chiar weight made law
body: In the settlement the silver weights of Muileann chiar are declared the only lawful weights on the roads of the island. Copies in bronze are sent to every waypoint house, and the house of Fearchar is paid for each.

title: The bronze-casters of Muileann dhearg
body: The bronze copies of the Muileann chiar weights are cast at Muileann dhearg, where a family of casters learned the craft from the silversmiths. They go on to cast bells, pins and lamp-bowls, and their lamp-bowls hold the Law's measure exactly.

title: Seonag Chrom
body: Seonag Chrom, granddaughter of Ruairidh Liath, rules at Cathair dhearg. She gives the clerks a room of their own in the red hall and a wage in silver, and from her reign the king-list is kept year by year and not reign by reign.

title: Inis bheag's school of letters
body: At Inis bheag on the Abhainn bheag in the north a teacher of the stag's people begins to teach letters to fishers' children who will never cut coal. It is the first teaching of letters for their own sake. The Hall's roll notes it, and adds that fish do not need reading.

title: Peigi nic Tormoid, clerk of the hall
body: Peigi nic Tormoid, of the line of Tormod Scrìobhaiche, is clerk of the hall at Cathair dhearg, the first whose own hand can be told from the others in the copies that survive. Her entries are short, and she never gives a reason where a fact will serve. Much of what is known of the middle of the age is in her hand, or copied from it.

title: The hawk-keepers of Seann Skell
body: At Seann Skell on the northern coast the fowler families keep a hawk in every household and feed it before the household eats. They burn their season's handful at dawn with the hawk on the wrist, for the flame, they say, is a hunger and should be fed as a hunger is fed. They call the hawk Mòd, the Hawk of Acaill, the grey hawk of time, as old as Fionntan mac Bòchra, eldest of men, who lived down the ages as a salmon, an eagle and a hawk; between them the two remember all things. From them Òrd an t-Seabhaig counts its beginning.

title: The hawk-rite spreads up the Abhainn ìseal
body: The dawn burning with the hawk spreads from Seann Skell on the northern shore up the Abhainn ìseal to Inis ìseal and Cnoc bheag. The Keeper at Dùn ìseal writes that the rite keeps the measure exactly and is therefore no concern of the Hall. Never again does the Hall say so of any rite.

title: The sting-oath at Ros bheag
body: The swearing on a scorpion's sting spreads from Baile àrsaidh up the western coast to Ros bheag, and the harbour court there takes it for every oath of trade. For the rest of the age a merchant who will not swear on the sting is not trusted in the western harbours.

title: The wolf-stone at Inis thais
body: The wolf-sworn road-guards of Caol leathan set a second wolf-stone at the shrine of Inis thais, and the keepers of the shrine begin to pray before it as well as to the drowned. The stone is white quartz, dragged from the mountain on a sledge at a cost greater than the shrine's.

title: The strike-books compared
body: Donnchadh mac Iain, a teacher of the stag's people at Cnoc bhàn, reads through the strike-books of many generations of apprentices. He finds that the coal breaks brighter in its colours for cutters in their later years than in their first, whatever their house, and argues that the vein answers practice. The elders answer that it answers what a cutter was born with, and that practice only shows it.

title: Donnchadh mac Iain leaves Cnoc bhàn
body: Donnchadh mac Iain and twenty-two of his hearers leave the house at Cnoc bhàn and settle at Muileann chaol, taking copies of the strike-books with them. The elders of Cnoc bhàn call it theft of the books. Donnchadh calls it copying, which it is.

title: The founding of the rival druid school
body: A school of druids breaks away, holding that the vein answers labour and not birth. Centuries later the Long War is fought over the same question in another shape.

title: The school at Muileann chaol
body: The school of Donnchadh mac Iain at Muileann chaol keeps strike-books of its own under a rule the elder school never had: a cutter's parentage is not written in the book at all. The two schools of the stag dispute by letter for the rest of the age, and both keep the letters.

title: The Hall hears the two schools
body: The Keeper Raonaid Dhubh hears both schools of the stag at Dùn ìseal and gives no ruling, saying that the vein has not asked the Hall to decide. The Hall's roll sets down the hearing and the refusal. No refusal of the Hall is more often cited.

title: What the people of Cnoc ghorm say of their stone
body: Scholars of the stag from Muileann chaol come to Calbh Cnoc ghorm and cannot read it. The people of Cnoc ghorm tell them the stone says: we did not come; we were here. The scholars write that the people say so. No later hand explains either the stone or the saying.

title: The digging at Làrach an Dùin
body: Men of Baile ghorm dig under the fallen walls of Làrach an Dùin for the riches the ruin was said to hold, and find ash and nothing else. The Keeper has them sentenced as if they had broken the Law, though no law covered it, and the sentence stands as the rule for all the old places after.

title: Baile ghorm's penance
body: The families of the diggers at Baile ghorm do penance by keeping in repair the road from their town to Tuam Cnoc dhìreach. In the southern hills it is called the diggers' road still.

title: Lachlann Bàn
body: Lachlann Bàn takes the red hall at Cathair dhearg. He builds granaries in every province seat that will have one, and makes a law about them, and for these he is remembered.

title: The shared-meal law written
body: Lachlann Bàn and the Keeper Raonaid Dhubh make the old unwritten custom law at Cathair dhearg: a household with grain above its winter's need gives the surplus to the common granary of its district before the storm season, and the granary feeds any household of the district that runs short. The successors of Peigi nic Tormoid write it into the rolls in full. It is the first law made by rìgh and Keeper together.

title: The granary of Cnoc mhòr
body: Cnoc mhòr builds its common granary under the new law before any other district, and sends word of it to Cathair dhearg. Lachlann Bàn sends back a silver ring for the reeve.

title: The common granaries of the mountain
body: Common granaries are raised under the new law in the mountain districts round Muileann chiar, where the households live by cutting and carrying and grow little of their own. The lowland districts grumble at filling them.

title: The granary at Cathair mhòr
body: A common granary is built within the old wall at Cathair mhòr, the first behind a town wall. The southern fishing towns, having no grain, send dried fish to it for their share.

title: Raiders in the eastern waters
body: Outlaws in boats raid the eastern fishing strands from the islets offshore, taking dried fish and nets. Sliochd Raghnaill arms its boats at Seann Tarr and burns two of the raiders' boats. The rest escape.

title: Oighrig nic Lachlainn
body: Oighrig nic Lachlainn, daughter of Lachlann Bàn, takes the hall at Cathair dhearg. She has no children, and before her reign is half done the houses begin to count their claims.

title: The late snow on the high passes
body: The weather-watchers on the cairns above Cnoc ghlas see snow lying on the high passes long past the opening of the galleries. The Hall keeps the galleries shut for the cutters' safety, and the mountain households wait.

title: The poor season in the mountain
body: The galleries open late and close early, and the coal carried down is a third of a common season's. The mountain households of Muileann gheal, Doire uaine and Àth dhìreach, who trade their carrying for grain, have nothing to trade, and by the season's end they are eating their seed.

title: The first recorded famine averted
body: A poor mining season brings three settlements near to starving. The shared-meal law, made a generation before, holds and saves them. It is the first true trial of the custom.

title: The granaries opened
body: Under the shared-meal law the common granaries of the mountain districts are opened at Muileann gheal. When they run low the granaries of Dùn dhearg and the southern coast send grain up the carriers' roads without being asked twice, and the carriers bear it for no fee. None in the three settlements is known to die of hunger that winter.

title: Àth dhìreach after the poor season
body: At Àth dhìreach, one of the three settlements the granaries fed, the carriers who brought up the grain are given the right to rest in any house of the town without payment for as long as they live. The last of them dies old, and the right with him.

title: The reeves of Dùn dhearg send the grain
body: The reeves of Dùn dhearg, who had withheld their accounts from Cathair dhearg for generations, open the old granaries of the house of Ìomhar to the mountain without waiting for an order. Oighrig nic Lachlainn writes that she would have given the order had they waited. The successor of Peigi nic Tormoid notes that they did not.

title: Death of Oighrig nic Lachlainn
body: Oighrig nic Lachlainn dies at Cathair dhearg with no heir of her body, and with her ends the line of Goraidh Mòr, as the list reckons it. The red hall is shut, and its clerks keep it.

title: The four houses meet
body: The Four Houses of custody meet at Dùn ìseal to choose a ruler, for no custom covers a hall without an heir. Sliochd Ìomhair claims it by blood, Sliochd Thormoid by the clerks, Sliochd Raghnaill by its boats. Sliochd Mhuirich, holding the Keeper's office, makes no claim.

title: The election of Gilleasbuig Mòr
body: The houses choose Gilleasbuig Mòr mac Tormoid of Seann Dunn, a grandson of the clerks' line, to hold the red hall. The Keeper sets the stone cup in his hands before the council, and so for the first time a ruler is made at Dùn ìseal. Sliochd Ìomhair consents, on condition that its graves at Dùn dhearg remain the burying-place of the kings.

title: Gilleasbuig Mòr at Cathair dhearg
body: Gilleasbuig Mòr takes the red hall. He keeps the clerks' office in the hands of his own house and has the king-list copied again from the beginning, with a line drawn beneath Oighrig nic Lachlainn. The line is in every later copy.

title: The shrine at Seann Dunn enlarged
body: Gilleasbuig Mòr enlarges his house's shrine at Seann Dunn into a temple with a court for pilgrims. The other houses say still that its coal-lamp burns fuller than the measure, and every season a Keeper's cutter is sent to try it.

title: Death of Gilleasbuig Mòr
body: Gilleasbuig Mòr dies at Cathair dhearg and is buried among the house of Ìomhar at Dùn dhearg, as was agreed. His son Tormod Òg follows him without a meeting of the houses, and none asks for one.

title: The gap in the list
body: Nine rulers of the house of Tormod reign between Tormod Òg and Anna Ruadh, and the king-list at Cathair dhearg gives their names and years and little else. The successors of Peigi nic Tormoid were diligent and brief; for these reigns the rolls tell mostly of harvests, tolls and the mending of bridges.

title: The bridge at Cathair dhearg widened
body: The bridge at Cathair dhearg is rebuilt a third time, wide enough now for a cart, for carts have come onto the lowland roads. The hearth-sign is cut again in the keystone. The span stands on the piers of Mòrag nan Rathad.

title: Riders on the lowland roads
body: The road-guards of Dùn dhearg begin to ride the lowland roads on the small horses of the southern grass country, and a guard can now reach a waypoint house before a quarrel there has cooled. They are the first riders whose names are kept, and for long the only ones.

title: The crossing at Ros fhionn repaired
body: A flood takes the eastern approach of Ailean Clachair's span above Ros fhionn, and it is mended. The masons find their founder's hearth-sign still sharp in the keystone, and leave it untouched.

title: The bridge at Dùn chrom
body: The masons' fellowship bridges the river below Dùn chrom, joining the southern road to the western without the long way round by Cathair dhearg. The toll is set at half the road-toll, and Cathair dhearg complains.

title: The bridge at Ceann àrsaidh
body: A bridge is built at the river town of Ceann àrsaidh, the fourth stone crossing of the lowlands. The masons' roll names the forty who built it, all of the fisher-kin of Sliochd Raghnaill, who had learned the craft while the boats lay idle.

title: The bridge at Doire mhin
body: The masons' fellowship builds a small bridge at Doire mhin to carry the southern road over a stream that floods each spring. Beside the hearth-sign in the keystone is cut the name of Beathag Clachair, who cut it: the first mason's mark known.

title: The far-off house
body: The waypoint house on the site of An Sligeanach Fad' às, the oldest house under the road-peace, is rebuilt in stone. It lies so far from any town that the carriers say one is never nearer to it than halfway, and from the saying it takes its name.

title: Fire-water on the northern road
body: The house on the northern road, on the site of An Leòmhann Buidhe, begins to serve a spirit distilled from barley that the carriers call fire-water. The Keepers rule that it is not a burning and no concern of theirs. The house's trade doubles.

title: Caol mhòr in the north-west
body: The fisher-families of the north-west gather at Caol mhòr under a headman of their own, and send tolls to Cathair dhearg only in the years the road-guard comes to take them. Little is written of the north-west in this age, and most of it is complaint of that.

title: Seal-oil from Ceann mhòr
body: Ceann mhòr on the north-west coast begins to trade seal-oil down the western coast to Ros bheag for silver rings, and its beacons burn it. For many generations the seal-oil lamps of the western harbours are the brightest light on Dia-thìr.

title: The high pastures of Muileann leathan
body: Herding families take the high pastures above Muileann leathan in the north and keep sheep there for the wool of Inis mhòr. They hold no right to the handful, have never held one, and are not counted in the census of hands.

title: Inis mhin on the northern shore
body: Inis mhin, a fishing harbour on the northern shore, comes into the rolls for the first time when its headman goes to the wool-fair of Inis mhòr to complain of the road-guard's toll. The complaint is written down in full, and it is all that is written of the town in this age.

title: The raid on the western strands
body: Raiders from the north-western waters take a season's dried fish from the strands of the north-western coast. The sting-sworn merchants of Ros bheag pay for two armed boats to watch the strands, and the raiders move north.

title: The second sighting
body: Two boats of Baile chrom tell of something vast moving beneath them in the north-western water, the second such sighting remembered. One boat does not come home. The wake that Baile chrom keeps for the first loss is kept now for both.

title: Round the islands
body: Boats of Sliochd Raghnaill sail from Seann Tarr round the offshore islands, Eilean ruadh, Eilean dhearg and Eilean fhada among them, and come home in one season. No crew of the age goes further from the coast than the islands, and none is known to have wished to.

title: Summer herders on Eilean ruadh
body: Families from the coast take sheep over to Eilean ruadh for the summer grazing and bring them back before the storms. They build turf shelters there, which later herders use again.

title: Anna Ruadh
body: Anna Ruadh of the house of Tormod takes the red hall at Cathair dhearg. She walks the whole circuit of the roads, the first ruler to do so since Mòrag nan Rathad, and she walks it twice.

title: Anna Ruadh at Am Buabhall Fortanach
body: On her first circuit Anna Ruadh stops at the house on the site of Am Buabhall Fortanach, where the War of the Roads was ended, and eats the jugged buffalo like a carrier. The keepers of the house tell of it still.

title: Anna Ruadh at the sunny house
body: On the eastern road Anna Ruadh lodges at the house on the site of An Taigh-òsta Grianach and grants its keepers a toll of their own for the upkeep of the road to Cnoc leathan, Slighe Cnoc leathan. No other waypoint house on the island holds a royal charter.

title: Anna Ruadh at Ceann mhin
body: At Ceann mhin on the south-eastern coast Anna Ruadh hears the quarrel of the fishers and the carriers over who may carry dried fish up to the mountain, and rules that both may. The fish going inland is doubled, and its price at Dùn ìseal halved.

title: The contest at Ceann leathan in stone
body: Anna Ruadh gives the road-guards' contest at Ceann leathan a stone-walled field, and for its prize a silver ring from the red hall. Fighters come to it from all the south, and the losers are fed at the crown's cost.

title: A wood-watcher in the red hall
body: Anna Ruadh keeps a wood-watcher from Coille Naomh Cnoc bheag in her household at Cathair dhearg to read the omens of the hall. So the rite of the wood-watchers, the rite of Macha, goddess of sovereignty and of horses, first comes to the capital. The Keeper sends a protest from Dùn ìseal, and the rolls give no answer.

title: Cathair dhomhain and the wood-watchers
body: The shrine at Cathair dhomhain, proud of its strict keeping of the Law, will take no wood-watcher, and its people say that the capital has given its omens to folk who sit in trees. From this the rivalry of the two towns takes a turn in matters of faith that it never loses.

title: Death of Anna Ruadh
body: Anna Ruadh dies at Cathair dhearg and is buried at Dùn dhearg among the house of Ìomhar and the kings of her own house. Her son Coinneach Bàn takes the hall.

title: Coinneach Bàn
body: Coinneach Bàn rules long and quietly from Cathair dhearg. In his reign the clerks of the hall begin to copy the rolls for the provinces, so that each province seat has its own copy of the laws. Several of those copies survive where the first writings are lost.

title: Seumas Bàn keeps the flame
body: Seumas Bàn of Sliochd Mhuirich is chosen Keeper. Reading the Hall's roll at Dùn ìseal he finds that more than half the Keepers of the age were of his own house, and has the fact struck from the preface. The unstruck copy survives.

title: The rites counted at Dùn ìseal
body: Seumas Bàn has the clerks of the Hall list every rite on the island that burns the handful and every one that lays claim to the vein, that the council may know what it keeps. The list holds the Hall's own rite, the ancestor-keeping of the old folk, the dawn-hawk of the north coast, the wood-watchers of the west, the wolf-sworn, the sting-oath, and both schools of the stag. The clerks write that a thousand years before no such list would have been needed.

title: The hawk-keepers refuse the Hall's cutter
body: The hawk-keepers of Seann Skell turn away the Hall's cutter who comes to try their measure, saying their measure is the hawk's, and the hawk is not the Keeper's. The cutter goes home with the refusal in writing. No rite had refused the trial of the measure outright before.

title: The wolf-sworn build a hall
body: The wolf-sworn of Caol leathan build a hall of their own about the white wolf-stone at the town gate, and swear oaths there that are no longer road-guards' oaths. The stone, they say, watches the whole island as the guard watches the road, and will cry out beneath the rightful king. From this hall comes Òrd na Cloiche, the order of the Stone, and the wolf-sworn begin to be called the Fianna.

title: The sting-oath at Seann Skell
body: At Seann Skell in the west the sting-oath of the harbour court becomes a creed. Its keepers hold that one power stings the liar wherever he may be, Manannan mac Lir, lord of the sea, and that the scorpion is but his sign; theirs is the first teaching on the island to call itself the only true one, and the Hall's roll sets it down as new. Thereafter the oath is sworn over a cup marked with the scorpion, Manannan's Cup of Truth, which is said to break in three at three lies spoken over it and to be made whole by three truths. Òrd Mhanannain dates itself from this court.

title: Seann Vell swears on the sting
body: Seann Vell, on the western coast below Cuan shean, takes up the sting-oath of its neighbours. Its shrine keeps a scorpion carved in yellow stone, the first image of the creature made for worship and not for swearing on.

title: The dark wood keeps its own rite
body: The wood-watchers of Coille Naomh Cnoc bheag cease to send to the Hall for judgement of their quarrels, and judge them under the trees. They hold that the black beast has two natures, one that keeps and one that devours, and that the vein has the same. The order of Macha afterwards tells of the two horses that drew one chariot, the black Dubh Sainglenn and the grey Liath Macha: two horses, one yoke.

title: The common root of the orders
body: The one folk-faith of the island begins plainly to divide into the several ways that later ages name apart: the orders of An Creideamh Sean, the Old Faith, and the hearth-keeping of Na Seann Spioradan, the Old Spirits. From this time the belief of the Dia-thìrich is no longer one.

title: The council divided by rite
body: The council at Dùn ìseal, which had sat by hearth and by house, begins to sit in companies by rite. Seumas Bàn complains that he keeps the flame now for eight peoples, each of whom thinks itself its only keeper. The seating holds for the rest of the age.

title: Allt an Àigh keeps its pilgrims
body: Pilgrims of every rite go on walking to Allt an Àigh in the right quarter of the moon; it is the one custom of the island that the Hall's list sets under no company. In one season the path from Caol shean is paved anew by pilgrims of four rites.

title: The springs at Muileann ruadh common to all
body: The keeper of the springs at Muileann ruadh rules that the sick of every rite shall be bathed without asking which. Her ruling is copied into the rolls of the provinces. It is the last ruling of the age on which every company of the council agrees.

title: Cnoc dhìreach's weavers
body: The town of Cnoc dhìreach in the east, on the carriers' road south of the springs, becomes known for a heavy undyed cloth that the carriers wear on the high passes. It is not the grave-keepers' village by the old tombs, and the rolls tell the two Cnoc dhìreachs apart by that cloth.

title: The dyers of Muileann bhàn
body: The dyers of Muileann bhàn in the eastern hills learn to fix a pale blue from a hill plant, and the carriers' cloth of all the mountain country is dyed there. The Keepers wear it undyed, and say so.

title: Muileann dhomhain's mill
body: A water-mill is built at Muileann dhomhain in the eastern hills to grind the grain of the common granaries of the mountain districts. The miller keeps one measure in sixteen, and the rolls call it fair.

title: The flood at Àth chiar
body: Rain on the eastern hills brings the river over the ford at Àth chiar, and it carries off the carriers' shelter and six of the townsfolk. The common granary of the district stands on a rise, is untouched, and feeds the town through the winter.

title: The oyster-beds of Seann Bhral
body: The people of Seann Bhral on the south-eastern coast begin to lay oyster-beds in the shallows, a craft that came, they say, with the name of their town. The Library's copy of the provincial roll sets down the claim and marks it doubtful.

title: Seann Vell's harbour
body: Seann Vell on the south-eastern coast grows into a city on the southern fishing and the silver of Muileann chiar brought down the eastern road. Its harbour is the first on the island with a stone quay.

title: The light at Tobar dhearg rebuilt
body: The old beacon at Tobar dhearg on the southern cape is rebuilt as a stone tower with the fire on its top, the first sea-light raised above the ground. It burns seal-oil of the north-west, carried the whole length of the island.

title: Muileann naomh's mill-shrine
body: At Muileann naomh on the southern coast a mill and a shrine share one roof, and the miller keeps the shrine's handful beside his millstones. The Keeper's cutter who comes to try it finds the measure kept and the flour good.

title: Dùn thais walled
body: Dùn thais in the eastern hills is walled, and a temple of the stag's people is raised within it, the first of theirs built in stone and not kept in a grove. The elder school at Cnoc bhàn sends it teachers.

title: The wool-fair of Inis mhòr
body: Inis mhòr holds a wool-fair at every shearing, and buyers come to it from all the northern coast and some from Cathair dhearg. Its silver is weighed on the Muileann chiar weights sent to the northern road.

title: Baile Mòr mhòr on the northern coast
body: Baile Mòr mhòr, on the northern coast west of Seann Toll, grows great enough on the fishing to send its own member to the council at Dùn ìseal. The Four Houses mislike it, and seat its member at the foot of the hall.

title: The northern boats at Seann Toll
body: The harbour at Seann Toll becomes the home of the northern fishing fleet. Its boatbuilders make the longest craft on the island, built for a day's run along the coast and never for open water.

title: Drought at Achadh shean
body: A dry summer burns the pastures round Achadh shean in the east, and by spring the district's common granary is empty. Grain is sent from Baile chaol and Cuan ruadh under the shared-meal law, and the district repays it over the harvests after.

title: Baile chaol's repayment
body: The rolls at Baile chaol set down the repayment of the drought grain by Achadh shean, measure by measure, to the last. The clerk adds that no such debt in the rolls was repaid in full before.

title: The panthers late
body: The great cats cross the southern road late, and fewer than the carriers remember. The weather-watchers read it for a hard winter, and are right. The Keepers note it without remark.

title: The watch-tower at Baile ruadh
body: A timber watch-tower is raised at Baile ruadh on the north-eastern coast to look out for raiders from the islands, manned by turns by the fisher-kin of Sliochd Raghnaill. It is the only tower of war the age builds.

title: Cuan ruadh's boats
body: The fishers of Cuan ruadh on the eastern coast give boats and men to the watch against the island raiders. In return Sliochd Raghnaill gives the town a place on the council at Dùn ìseal beside its own seat.

title: The drowned-feast at Inis chrom
body: At Inis chrom on the western coast the families of the drowned hold a feast on the shore each year and set an empty place for each of the lost. The custom spreads to the harbours northward as far as Seann Warr.

title: The potters of Baile ghorm
body: Potters at Baile ghorm on the south-western coast begin to fire a hard red ware of the local clay, and their jars carry the oil and grain of the western road. Sherds of it lie on every waypoint-house site the Library's surveyors have walked.

title: Cnoc àrsaidh's kilns
body: Potters of Baile ghorm set up new kilns at Cnoc àrsaidh in the south-west, where the clay is better and the wood nearer. There the red ware of the western road is made for the rest of the age.

title: Cathair fhada grows
body: Families leaving the crowded harbours about Cathair dhearg settle at Cathair fhada on the southern coast and raise its long street along the ridge. They bring a wood-watcher with them, and a copy of the laws.

title: Cnoc naomh's ancestor-shrine
body: The people of Cnoc naomh keep a shrine to the ancestors and to the sìth of the hill in the old folk way, with no hawk, wolf, sting or stag in it. The Hall's list of rites names them among the keepers of the old reverence, which by now is a company of its own.

title: Mòr nic Coinnich crowned
body: Mòr nic Coinnich, granddaughter of Coinneach Bàn, takes the red hall at Cathair dhearg. The Keeper Catrìona nic Mhuirich sets the stone cup in her hands at Dùn ìseal, as the houses had done for Gilleasbuig Mòr. Hers is the last name written in the king-list of the Holy Age.

title: The Hall's roll at the close of the age
body: At the close of the age the Keepers' roll holds one hundred and forty names, from Beathag Bhàn to Catrìona nic Mhuirich, and the king-list more than ninety, from Goraidh Mòr to Mòr nic Coinnich. The Small-Burning Law is unchanged in any word since the stone cup of Fionnlagh Dall, and the cup stands yet on the threshold of Talla na Lasrach at Dùn ìseal.

title: The last age of even population
body: So ends the Holy Age. The chroniclers of after days look back on it with some unease: it is the last time in the history of Dia-thìr that no family's lives ran longer than any other's.

title: Land is found
body: Word comes of a land across the open water, where no people like the Dia-thìrich dwell. Who first found it is not told.

title: The tidings at Cathair dhearg
body: Three crews from the western harbours bring word of the far land to the hall of Queen Beathag nic Dhòmhnaill, daughter of Mòr nic Coinnich, at Cathair dhearg. None claims to have been first. The queen's scribe takes down all three tellings; they agree on the coast and on nothing else.

title: The Choosing
body: A vote, or what the later chroniclers call a vote, settles who will go. Only the willing go; no lots are drawn and none are pressed.

title: The roll of the willing
body: The harbour scribes of Seann Skell open a roll of those who mean to go, written by household and not by name, on boards in the harbour-house. A later hand notes that names were struck out as often as they were added.

title: The queen neither commands nor forbids
body: Queen Beathag declares that the crown will send no one across the water and keep no one back. Within the season her younger sister, Mòrag nic Dhòmhnaill, enters her own household on the roll at Seann Skell.

title: The custodians count the cost
body: The vein-house above Muileann dhearg, keeper of Crom's stone and heir to the Keepers' Hall at Dùn ìseal where Brìde's flame was first bound, counts the households of the coal-right that have entered the roll. The custody-book makes it nearly one in five, and says the count was made twice, for the first figure was not believed.

title: The ships are built
body: The shipwrights of the island, used to small coasting craft, build ships to keep the open sea, the first in the memory of Dia-thìr.

title: Alasdair Saor lays the first keel
body: On the river strand below Seann Skell the shipwright Alasdair mac Iain, called Alasdair Saor, lays down the first deep-keeled hull built on Dia-thìr. Until then the island's boats were sewn-plank coasters that never lay a night out of sight of land.

title: The oaks of Doire fhionn
body: The oak grove that named Doire fhionn is felled for the keels of the fleet and drawn to the coast on ox-sleds. It never grew again, and the village kept a name it had no more cause for.

title: The shipwrights' fellowship
body: Alasdair Saor gathers the wrights of the Seann Skell strand into one fellowship, and binds each apprentice for seven years after the manner of the vein custodians. The custody-book names it Comann nan Saor-luinge, the fellowship of the ship-wrights.

title: The trial hull lost off Ros àrsaidh
body: The first finished hull is taken down the Abhainn naomh and out past Ros àrsaidh, where the ships of Inis àrsaidh put to sea, for trial in open water. It founders in a following sea and eleven are drowned. Alasdair Saor alters the setting of the keel, and every later hull of the fleet is built to the new pattern.

title: The rope-walks of Cuan shean
body: Cuan shean lays out long rope-walks along its harbour front and gives all its hemp fields to cordage for the fleet. Its rope trade lasts some centuries beyond the Sundering.

title: The sail-cloth levy
body: Every weaving household in Siorrachd Baile àrsaidh owes a set length of close-woven sail-cloth, scored on tally-sticks at the shire seat. The tallies survive; how many paid is not known.

title: The star-lore of Cuan ruadh
body: The old steersmen of Cuan ruadh on the eastern coast, the only sailors of the island who had ever held a course by night, teach the pilots of the fleet to steer by the stars. Their lore was written down only in part, and that part is lost.

title: The willing choose their leaders
body: The households of the roll meet at Seann Skell and choose Mòrag nic Dhòmhnaill, the queen's sister, and Fearchar mac Ruairidh, a custodian of the vein, to lead them. The custody-book records the choice; how it was made is not told.

title: The handful for the new hearth
body: The vein-house rules that each departing ship may carry one sealed measure of the coal, no more than a single household may burn in a season under the Small-Burning Law. It is the only writing in the custody-book addressed to those who were leaving.

title: The west quay lengthened
body: Masons from the capital lengthen the west quay at Seann Skell with dressed stone, so that the deep hulls may lie alongside at low water. On these stones the later rite was held.

title: The strife over the grain
body: Strife over how much of the island's stored grain the ships may take all but ends the venture. Within a season it is settled; how is not recorded.

title: Àth shean shuts its granaries
body: In the strife over the fleet's grain Tormod mac Coinnich, reeve of the granaries at Àth shean, bars the store-houses and sets a watch on them until the matter is settled. He holds no office afterward.

title: Grain down Abhainn dhomhain
body: The strife settled, grain barges go down Abhainn dhomhain to the capital, on by the coast to Ros àrsaidh, and up the Abhainn naomh to Seann Skell. A tally-keeper at Drochaid Cathair dhearg counts forty-one barges passing.

title: The fleet assembled
body: The fleet lies complete at Seann Skell. The custody-book gives nineteen hulls; a later hand in the margin makes it twenty-one. Which is right has never been settled.

title: The night of lamps
body: On the last night before the sailing every house on the Seann Skell waterfront sets a lamp on its sill and keeps it burning till morning. It is the first custom of the Sundering written down as a custom, and the town kept it long after its cause had become a tale.

title: The Setting-Out
body: The willing sail west. The chronicles of the island fall silent on them as the ships clear the harbour; the Dia-thìrich tell that the fleet sailed into Manannan's mist, toward the Otherworld.

title: The sunwise turn
body: Before going down the Abhainn naomh to the open sea the fleet goes once round the river pool of Seann Skell sunwise, diosal, for luck, and the watchers on the quay count the hulls as they pass. The harbour scribe's account ends at the foot of the pool.

title: The years counted from the turn
body: Donnchadh mac Thormoid, scribe of the vein-house, begins to number the years from the sunwise turn at Seann Skell, and calls them the years of the Diosal. The count is his; the crown's scribes take it up a generation later.

title: Tidings reach Seann Skell
body: Tidings of the fleet reach Seann Skell, by what road or whose mouth is not told. The harbour scribe copies them in a shaking hand; the copy came down to later keepers water-stained and lacking its end.

title: Two landfalls
body: Such broken tidings as come back tell of two coasts reached, not one. In this telling lies the seed of the two peoples that came after.

title: Mòrag's line struck
body: Queen Beathag strikes her sister Mòrag and Mòrag's children from the succession, as no longer on Dia-thìr. The act stands without comment between a grain ruling and the mending of a bridge.

title: The thinning
body: Cut off from the vein, the strength the crossing asked of them fades in the children of those who went. By the third generation over the water nothing is left that Dia-thìr would know.

title: The custodians' second count
body: The vein-house counts again the households of the coal-right and sets the loss at one hand in five. Beside it Donnchadh mac Thormoid writes that the vein answers no differently for those who stayed.

title: The Mourning Custom
body: Dia-thìr sets in order a rite of mourning for the departed, neither wholly grief nor wholly feast. In a far later age it was used again, uneasily, for a very different leaving.

title: The white sorrow first kept at court
body: Queen Beathag mourns her sister in undyed wool, with one place left empty at a meal that is neither feast nor fast. The court calls it an Tùrsa Geal, the white sorrow, and within a generation it is kept in every harbour town of the island.

title: The custodians fewer
body: With part of the coal-bound folk gone, the Dia-thìrich order themselves anew about a smaller and closer class of custodians. From this shape every later nobility descends.

title: The seven houses of custody
body: The custodian households that remain are gathered into seven houses, each answerable to the vein-house for its share of the coal and of the measured burning: Clann Mhuirich, Clann Fhearchair, Clann Ìomhair, Clann Raghnaill, Clann Thormoid, Clann Choinnich and Clann Lachlainn. Here for the first time the right to the coal passes by house and not by apprenticeship.

title: Death of Queen Beathag
body: Queen Beathag nic Dhòmhnaill dies at Cathair dhearg, the last ruler of Dia-thìr who saw the fleet. Her son Raghnall mac Uilleim is crowned in the same hall.

title: The rite of the empty harbour
body: A rite grows up about the quay the ships sailed from. It is still kept, lessened, on a day that none can now date truly.

title: The harbour at half trade
body: The harbour-master of Seann Skell finds his berths at half their old use, for the fishing households that crewed the fleet are gone. The rope-walks of Cuan shean turn off hands for the first time.

title: The second silence
body: There is a rumour of a second, smaller crossing, with fewer ships and no word of where they went. Nothing that survives confirms or denies it.

title: The watch at Ceann mhòr
body: The fishing families of Ceann mhòr on the north-west coast keep a watch from the headland for returning sails, household by household in turn. The watch lapses within a generation. No sail is seen.

title: The west quay renamed
body: The quay the ships sailed from is given a new name, so that common trade might go on under the old one without the memory. It is an early and quiet forgetting, made on purpose.

title: Cidhe an Diosail
body: The departure berth is entered in the harbour rolls of Seann Skell as Cidhe an Diosail, the quay of the sunwise turn. The name Cidhe an Iar passes to the new fish-wharf at the north end of the strand, and within a few years the fishers use it without a thought.

title: Roghnaich takes its narrow sense
body: In the custody-book the verb roghnaich, to choose, begins to stand with no object, meaning to have chosen the crossing. The scribes of the next century use it so without explaining it, the surest sign that it had passed into common speech.

title: The first generation that never saw the fleet
body: Children born soon after the Setting-Out grow up never having seen the harbour with those ships in it. To them the leaving is already history.

title: Death of Alasdair Saor
body: Alasdair Saor, who laid the first deep keel, dies at Seann Skell. His last work was a coasting trader of the old sewn-plank kind, built for a fish merchant of Inis àrsaidh.

title: The shipwrights' fellowship ends
body: No more sea-going ships being wanted, the fellowship that built the fleet of the Sundering quietly breaks up. Its craft is half forgotten by the time anyone needs it again.

title: The keel-moulds burned
body: In a hard season the patterns and moulds of the broken fellowship, kept in a shed on the strand at Seann Skell, are burned for firewood. The harbour-master notes the loss of the shed and not of what was in it.

title: The mountain divided among the houses
body: The seven houses draw lots at the vein-house for the galleries each will keep, and the vein-house confirms each its Small-Burning measure. The lot-stones were kept in a bag at Muileann dhearg and shown to visitors for centuries after.

title: The coppice law of Doire fhionn
body: The great oaks gone to the fleet, the shire of Doire fhionn forbids the felling of any living oak without the reeve's mark and begins to cut its woods by coppice. The law spreads to every shire with a Doire in its name.

title: The lamps kept at Seann Skell
body: The waterfront of Seann Skell keeps the night of lamps each year on the eve of the rite of the empty harbour. The children are told the lamps are for ships coming home, and the priests do not gainsay it.

title: Death of Donnchadh mac Thormoid
body: Donnchadh mac Thormoid, the vein-house scribe who began the count of years, dies at Muileann dhearg. His last entry is the season's burning of coal, household by household, in the same hand as his first.

title: Raghnall dies; Ìomhar crowned
body: King Raghnall mac Uilleim dies at Cathair dhearg after a long and quiet reign, and his son Ìomhar mac Raghnaill is crowned. The custody-book gives Raghnall's reign a single line.

title: The silversmiths of Muileann chiar
body: Silver of the seam at Muileann chiar, mined since the Holy Age, is wrought into neck-rings for the heads of the seven houses. The smiths' fellowship of the seam, heirs of Sliochd Fhearchair, keeps its craft within four families.

title: Inis mhòr's grain fleet
body: Inis mhòr in the north builds barges to carry grain down the Abhainn ghorm to Caol bheag, and from Ros chiar at the river mouth west along the coast to Cnoc bheag. They are sewn-plank boats of the old kind, and none lies a night out of sight of land.

title: The coughing sickness at Caol fhiadhaich
body: A coughing sickness runs through Caol fhiadhaich on the south-west coast and kills some two hundred before it burns out. The shared meal is kept throughout, and the reeve holds that it saved the rest.

title: Am Buabhall Fortanach rebuilt in stone
body: The old road-house of Am Buabhall Fortanach burns to its footings, and its keeper, Eilidh nic Chaluim, rebuilds it in stone. It is already known for its jugged buffalo.

title: The spirit-house at Dùn ìseal
body: The keepers of the Old Spirits, the faith of the hearths, raise a house for the ancestors at Dùn ìseal, and cut the names of the dead of the eastern shires on wooden posts. The posts are cut anew each generation as the old ones rot.

title: Ìomhar dies without an heir
body: King Ìomhar mac Raghnaill dies at Cathair dhearg with no living child, and with him ends the line of Beathag. The heads of the seven houses are summoned to the capital to name a king.

title: Fearchar mac Lachlainn chosen
body: The heads of the houses choose Fearchar mac Lachlainn of Baile Mòr dhomhain, of Clann Fhearchair, and he is crowned at Cathair dhearg. He is the first king made by the custodian houses and not by descent.

title: A court at Baile Mòr dhomhain
body: King Fearchar keeps his court part of each year at Baile Mòr dhomhain, near the mountain, that he may take counsel of the vein-house without a journey. The double court lasts as long as his house.

title: The fishers of Àth fhiadhaich
body: After a season of losses the fishing families of Àth fhiadhaich join in one fellowship to share boats and nets. It is the first fishers' fellowship on the east coast.

title: Fearchar Donn crowned
body: Fearchar mac Lachlainn dies, and his son, called Fearchar Donn, is crowned at Cathair dhearg without dispute.

title: Gormshuil of the Hawk
body: At Cnoc bheag, where the dawn-hawk rite of the Holy Age is still kept, the priestess Gormshuil nic Artair teaches that the hawk of the rite is Mòd, the Hawk of Acaill, as old as Fionntan mac Bòchra, eldest of men, and remembering all things with him. The vein, she teaches, is the Hungry Hawk, to be fed the measured handful and no more, for a hawk overfed will not hunt and a hawk starved will turn on the hand. Her followers gather the old rite into the first house of Òrd an t-Seabhaig, the order of the Hawk of Acaill.

title: The hawk-house at Ros gheal
body: Gormshuil's pupils found a second house of the Hawk at Ros gheal. Its priests take charge of the measured burning for all the country between Ros gheal on the coast and Cnoc bheag up the river.

title: Flood at Seann Vell
body: In a wet spring the river at Seann Vell on the south-east coast breaks its banks and carries away the lower mills. The mill-wrights build them again on the higher bank.

title: The sayings of Gormshuil written
body: After Gormshuil's death her sayings are written at Cnoc bheag as Leabhar an t-Seabhaig, the Book of the Hawk. The copyist, Ùisdean mac Pàdraig, marks every saying he did not hear from her own mouth, and these are the greater part.

title: The storm that took Seann Toll's boats
body: A northern storm, named Am Fuath Mòr in the harbour rolls, breaks the harbour wall of Seann Toll and sinks forty boats at their moorings. Eighteen fishers drown.

title: Seann Toll walls its harbour again
body: Seann Toll builds its harbour wall again, higher and with a hooked end, to a plan the reeve had from the masons of the capital. The wall stands through every storm of this age.

title: The walls of Dùn dhearg
body: Clann Ìomhair, who hold the land about Dùn dhearg in the eastern hills, wall it in stone. These are the first walls on the island raised by a custodian house and not by the crown.

title: Queen Sìleas's measures
body: Sìleas nic Fhearchair, crowned after her father Fearchar Donn, fixes one measure for grain across the island, the firlot of Cathair dhearg, so that barter between shires need not begin with a quarrel over the size of a basket. Firlots of oak bound with iron are sent to every shire seat.

title: Tally-houses in the royal granaries
body: Queen Sìleas sets a tally-house in each royal granary, where every exchange of grain for cloth, salt or labour is cut on paired sticks, one for each party. It is the first reckoning of trade across the whole island, and it runs without coin.

title: The market charter of Cathair fhada
body: Queen Sìleas grants Cathair fhada a market on its ridge at every full moon, with a tally-house for the south; it is the first market right cut on paired sticks. The merchants of the long city carry the honey, hemp, wax and pots of the south to the capital, and begin to go as one company to the harvest fair at Muileann òg.

title: Drochaid Cathair dhearg widened
body: The old stone bridge over Abhainn dhomhain at Cathair dhearg is widened for two carts to pass. Queen Sìleas's name is cut on the downstream parapet, and may still be read there.

title: The crossing days of the panthers
body: In the southern hills near Imrich nam Pantar the herders keep the panther roads clear on the days the great cats cross, and drive their flocks off the paths beforehand. The crossing days are the first thing the southern shires agree on in writing.

title: An Leòmhann Buidhe on the north road
body: An Leòmhann Buidhe, a road-house on the northern mining road, serves the coal-carters oatcakes fried in linseed oil, and fire water. Its keeper is fined for watering the fire water.

title: The house of disputation at Dùn thais
body: Coinneach mac Mhàrtainn, a druid of the schools of Flidais, lady of the deer, founds a house of disputation at Dùn thais, where the old question of the schools, Carson an làmh seo?, why the vein answers some hands and not others, is argued by rule. Pupils come from as far as Caol bheag.

title: Coinneach's question
